section.heading: 6.5. Average Value of a Function
section.paragraph: It is easy to calculate the average value of finitely many numbers $$y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}$$ :
$$y_{avg} = \frac{y_{1} + y_{2} + \cdot \cdot \cdot + y_{n}}{n}$$

But how do we compute the average temperature during a day if infinitely many temperature readings are possible? Figure 1 shows the graph of a temperature function $$T(t)$$ , where $$t$$ is measured in hours and $$T$$ in $${}_{}^{}{}$$ , and a guess at the average temperature, $$T_{avg}$$ .

section.paragraph: In general, let’s try to compute the average value of a function $$y = {f(x)}$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . We start by dividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ equal subintervals, each with length $$\Delta x = \left( {b - a} \right) \slash n$$ . Then we choose points $$x_{1}^{*},\ldots,x_{n}^{*}$$ in successive subintervals and calculate the average of the numbers $$f\left( x_{1}^{*} \right),\ldots,f\left( x_{n}^{*} \right)$$ :
$$\frac{f\left( x_{1}^{*} \right) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f\left( x_{n}^{*} \right)}{n}$$

(For example, if $$f$$ represents a temperature function and $$n = 24$$ , this means that we take temperature readings every hour and then average them.) Since $$\Delta x = \left( {b - a} \right) \slash n$$ , we can write $$n = \left( {b - a} \right) \slash \Delta x$$ and the average value becomes

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{f(x_{1}^{*}) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f(x_{n}^{*})}{\frac{b - a}{\Delta x}} = \frac{1}{b - a}\lbrack f(x_{1}^{*}) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f(x_{n}^{*})\rbrack\Delta x} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f(x_{1}^{*}) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f(x_{n}^{*})}{\frac{b - a}{\Delta x}}} = \frac{1}{b - a}\left\lbrack {f{(x_{1}^{*})}\Delta x + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f{(x_{n}^{*})}\Delta x} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f(x_{1}^{*}) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f(x_{n}^{*})}{\frac{b - a}{\Delta x}}} = \frac{1}{b - a}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f{(x_{i}^{*})}\Delta x}}} \end{array}$$

If we let $$n$$ increase, we would be computing the average value of a large number of closely spaced values. (For example, we would be averaging temperature readings taken every minute or even every second.) The limiting value is
$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{b - a}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{{f\left( x_{i}^{*} \right)}\Delta x = \frac{1}{b - a}{\int_{a}^{b}{{f(x)}dx}}}}$$
by the definition of a definite integral.
Therefore we define the average value of $$\mathbf{f}$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ as
$$f_{avg} = \frac{1}{b - a}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}$$
For a positive function, we can think of this definition as saying
$$\frac{area}{width} = {average height}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the average value of the function $${f(x)} = 1 + x^{2}$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack$$ .
example.heading: Solution

section.paragraph: If $$T(t)$$ is the temperature at time $$t$$ , we might wonder if there is a specific time when the temperature is the same as the average temperature. For the temperature function graphed in Figure 1, we see that there are two such times—just before noon and just before midnight. In general, is there a number $$c$$ at which the value of a function $$f$$ is exactly equal to the average value of the function, that is, $${f(c)} = f_{avg}$$ ? The following theorem says that this is true for continuous functions.

section.paragraph: The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals is a consequence of the Mean Value Theorem for derivatives and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. The proof is outlined in Exercise 28.

The geometric interpretation of the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals is that, for positive functions $$f$$ , there is a number $$c$$ such that the rectangle with base $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ and height $$f(c)$$ has the same area as the region under the graph of $$f$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ . (See Figure 2 and the more picturesque interpretation in the margin note.)

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Show that the average velocity of a car over a time interval $$\left\lbrack {t_{1},t_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ is the same as the average of its velocities during the trip.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: If $$s(t)$$ is the displacement of the car at time $$t$$ , then, by definition, the average velocity of the car over the interval is
$$\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \frac{s\left( t_{2} \right) - s\left( t_{1} \right)}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$
On the other hand, the average value of the velocity function on the interval is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\upsilon_{avg} = {\frac{1}{t_{2} - t_{1}}{\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}{\upsilon{(t)}dt = \frac{1}{t_{2} - t_{1}}{\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}{s^{\prime}{(t)}dt}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon_{ave}} = {\frac{1}{t_{2} - t_{1}}\left\lbrack {s\left( t_{2} \right) - s\left( t_{1} \right)} \right\rbrack \left( \text{by the Net Change Theorem} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon_{ave}} = {\frac{s\left( t_{2} \right) - s\left( t_{1} \right)}{t_{2} - t_{1}} = {average velocity}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Applied Project Calculus and Baseball
section.paragraph: In this project we explore three of the many applications of calculus to baseball. The physical interactions of the game, especially the collision of ball and bat, are quite complex and their models are discussed in detail in a book by Robert Adair, The Physics of Baseball, 3d ed. (New York, 2002).

image.alt: Details A two-dimensional rendering of the positions of a baseball and bat. The figure consists of a rectangle, labeled Batter's box, and the positions of a baseball and a bat. The ball travels horizontally rightward and strikes the bat positioned vertically at approximately the center of the box. Silhouettes of the bat are drawn before and after the ball strikes the bat. The knob of the bat follows a concave down arc with the silhouettes placed close together and leaning leftward initially and then more far apart and leaning rightward and then left as we proceed to the right.

list.item: It may surprise you to learn that the collision of baseball and bat lasts only about a thousandth of a second. Here we calculate the average force on the bat during this collision by first computing the change in the ball’s momentum. The momentum $$p$$ of an object is the product of its mass $$m$$ and its velocity $$\upsilon$$ , that is, $$p = m\upsilon$$ . Suppose an object, moving along a straight line, is acted on by a force $$F = F(t)$$ that is a continuous function of time. Show that the change in momentum over a time interval $$\left\lbrack {t_{0},t_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ is equal to the integral of $$F$$ from $$t_{0}$$ to $$t_{1}$$ ; that is, show that $$p\left( t_{1} \right) - p\left( t_{0} \right) = {\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}{F{(t)}dt}}$$ This integral is called the impulse of the force over the time interval. A pitcher throws a $$90{-mi} \slash h$$ fastball to a batter, who hits a line drive directly back to the pitcher. The ball is in contact with the bat for $$0.001$$ s and leaves the bat with velocity $$110{mi} \slash h$$ . A baseball weighs $$5$$ oz and, in US Customary units, its mass is measured in slugs: $$m = w \slash g$$ , where $$g = 32{ft} \slash s^{2}$$ . Find the change in the ball’s momentum. Find the average force on the bat.

In this problem we calculate the work required for a pitcher to throw a $$90{-mi} \slash h$$ fastball by first considering kinetic energy. The kinetic energy $$K$$ of an object of mass $$m$$ and velocity $$\upsilon$$ is given by $$K = \frac{1}{2}m\upsilon^{2}$$ . Suppose an object of mass $$m$$ , moving in a straight line, is acted on by a force $$F = F(s)$$ that depends on its position $$s$$ . According to Newton’s Second Law $$F(s) = ma = m\frac{d\upsilon}{dt}$$ where $$a$$ and $$\upsilon$$ denote the acceleration and velocity of the object. Show that the work done in moving the object from a position $$s_{0}$$ to a position $$s_{1}$$ is equal to the change in the object’s kinetic energy; that is, show that $$W = {\int_{s_{0}}^{s_{1}}{F(s)ds = \frac{1}{2}m\upsilon_{1}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}m\upsilon_{0}^{2}}}$$ where $$\upsilon_{0} = \upsilon{(s_{0})}$$ and $$\upsilon_{1} = \upsilon{(s_{1})}$$ are the velocities of the object at the positions $$s_{0}$$ and $$s_{1}$$ . Hint: By the Chain Rule, $$m\frac{d\upsilon}{dt} = m\frac{d\upsilon}{ds}\frac{ds}{dt} = m\upsilon\frac{d\upsilon}{ds}$$ How many foot-pounds of work does it take to throw a baseball at a speed of $$90{mi} \slash h$$ ?

An outfielder fields a baseball $$280$$ ft away from home plate and throws it directly to the catcher with an initial velocity of $$100{ft} \slash s$$ . Assume that the velocity $$\upsilon(t)$$ of the ball after $$t$$ seconds satisfies the differential equation $$d\upsilon \slash dt = - \frac{1}{10}\upsilon$$ because of air resistance. How long does it take for the ball to reach home plate? (Ignore any vertical motion of the ball.) The manager of the team wonders whether the ball will reach home plate sooner if it is relayed by an infielder. The shortstop can position himself directly between the outfielder and home plate, catch the ball thrown by the outfielder, turn, and throw the ball to the catcher with an initial velocity of $$105{ft} \slash s$$ . The manager clocks the relay time of the shortstop (catching, turning, throwing) at half a second. How far from home plate should the shortstop position himself to minimize the total time for the ball to reach home plate? Should the manager encourage a direct throw or a relayed throw? What if the shortstop can throw at $$115{ft} \slash s$$ ? For what throwing velocity of the shortstop does a relayed throw take the same time as a direct throw?

section.heading: Applied Project Where to Sit at the Movies
section.paragraph: A movie theater has a screen that is positioned $$10$$ ft off the floor and is $$25$$ ft high. The first row of seats is placed $$9$$ ft from the screen and the rows are set $$3$$ ft apart. The floor of the seating area is inclined at an angle of $$\alpha = 20^{{^\circ}}$$ above the horizontal and the distance up the incline that you sit is $$x$$ . The theater has $$21$$ rows of seats, so $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 60$$ . Suppose you decide that the best place to sit is in the row where the angle $$\theta$$ subtended by the screen at your eyes is a maximum. Let’s also suppose that your eyes are $$4$$ ft above the floor, as shown in the figure. (In Exercise 4.7.84 we looked at a simpler version of this problem, where the floor is horizontal, but this project involves a more complicated situation and requires technology.)

image.alt: Details A two dimensional rendering of the position of a person's chair in a movie theatre. On the left, there is a vertical screen of height 25 feet positioned 10 feet above the ground. At a distance of 9 feet from the wall with the screen, a ramp slopes upward to the right at an angle alpha from the ground. Shadowed silhouettes of chairs are placed at regular intervals on the ramp. The solid image of a person on a chair is positioned near the top of the ramp. The height of the solid image is 4 feet. From the top and the bottom of the screen, dashed line segments extend rightward, sloping downward and upward, respectively, to meet the person's eyes. The angle between the dashed line segments is labeled theta.

list.item: Show that $$\theta = \arccos\left( \frac{a^{2} + b^{2} - 625}{2ab} \right)$$ where $$a^{2} = \left( {9 + x\cos\alpha} \right)^{2} + \left( {31 - x\sin\alpha} \right)^{2}$$ and $$b^{2} = \left( {9 + x\cos\alpha} \right)^{2} + \left( {x\sin\alpha - 6} \right)^{2}$$
Use a graph of $$\theta$$ as a function of $$x$$ to estimate the value of $$x$$ that maximizes $$\theta$$ . In which row should you sit? What is the viewing angle $$\theta$$ in this row?
Use a computer algebra system to differentiate $$\theta$$ and find a numerical value for the solution of the equation $$d\theta \slash dx = 0$$ . Does this value confirm your result in Problem 2?

Use the graph of $$\theta$$ to estimate the average value of $$\theta$$ on the interval $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 60$$ . Then use a computer algebra system to compute the average value. Compare with the maximum and minimum values of $$\theta$$ .
